list.listitem: Iodine deficiency remains the most common preventable cause of nontoxic multinodular goiter and adequate iodine intake is effective in decreasing its incidence. B

Clinical assessment and measurement of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) are essential tools in the evaluation of goiter; ultrasonography is recommended to characterize the size and nodularity and to assess suspicious features of malignancy. B
For patients with asymptomatic nontoxic goiter in whom the risk of malignancy has been largely excluded, observation and follow-up are adequate measures. C
For patients with compressive symptoms or in whom the risk of malignancy cannot be ruled out, surgery is the treatment of choice. B

For large goiters in which the risk of malignancy is minimal and the risk of surgery is significant, radioiodine ablation with or without recombinant TSH stimulation is a reasonable and effective alternative approach to surgery. B

background.definition: Goiter is a term that denotes enlargement of the thyroid gland. This enlargement may be diffuse or asymmetrical, homogeneous or nodular, and associated with hyperthyroidism (toxic) or euthyroidism (nontoxic). This section will cover homogeneous and nontoxic multinodular goiter. Thyroid nodules, hypothyroidism, and hyperthyroidism, including toxic multinodular goiter, are covered in other sections.

list.listitem: Prevalence depends on the iodine status of the population and the method of detection used; there is significant regional variation.
In iodine-sufficient areas, using palpation, the prevalence of goiter is approximately 1% to 7% with much higher prevalence in women than in men (ratio 4.5:1).
In iodine-sufficient areas, the prevalence of single and multiple thyroid nodules is 0.8% and 5.3%, respectively.
In iodine-deficient areas, the prevalence of goiter can be as high as 15%.
Ultrasonography and autopsy studies reported much higher prevalence of thyroid nodules, ranging between 17% and 67%.
The prevalence of nodules increases with age, whereas the prevalence of diffuse goiter seems to decrease with age.
Iodine deficiency is the most common cause of goiter worldwide.
Goitrogens.
Genetic defects in thyroid hormone synthesis (dyshormonogenesis).

There is a heterogeneous response of thyroid follicular cells to different stimuli. The cause of this heterogeneity is unknown, but might be due to genetic factors and the acquisition of new inheritable characteristics.
The size and pathology vary considerably from small goiter with tiny nodules to massive goiter with nodules of different size, function, and histopathology.
Early in the process of goitrogenesis, goiter is usually diffuse; long-standing goiters tend to be nodular. Hemorrhage and necrosis may occur in some nodules.
Goitrogens in food or the environment may initiate or exacerbate the process of goitrogenesis.

In some cases, genetic defects in thyroid hormone synthesis lead to chronic stimulation by TSH and goiter formation. Other growth factors such as insulin-like growth factor-1 and epidermal growth factor may contribute in some cases.
Routine screening for multinodular goiter is not recommended; multinodular goiter is either discovered incidentally or patients present with asymptomatic lower neck swelling. C
Adequate iodine dietary intake is important to prevent the development of endemic goiter. B
Salt iodization programs have been shown to be quite effective in decreasing the incidence of goiter, though the effect of fortifying foods other than salt is unclear.B
In the early stages of goitrogenesis when the goiter is still small and diffuse, low-dose iodine supplementation can lead to a regression in the size of the goiter. C
Clinical assessment is important for subsequent diagnostic work-up. B
Measure serum TSH to assess thyroid function. C
Neck ultrasonography is indicated to assess intrinsic features of the goiter and nodules. B
Fine-needle aspiration biopsy is indicated for nodules that are dominant, unusually firm, or have suspicious features on ultrasonography. B
Imaging studies may be indicated in certain cases to assess the extent of goiter and its relationship to and effects on adjacent structures. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Diffuse bilateral enlargement of the thyroid gland
Diffuse, frequently huge goiter starting in childhood, positive family history
Usually a single nodule, invasive features or lymphadenopathy
Usually associated with painful thyroid and is transient

list.listitem: Physical examination is fairly good for detecting goiter but has limitations. Goiter can be detected as a lower mid-neck swelling that moves with swallowing.
Goiter is usually bilateral and nodular but can be nodular or diffuse, symmetrical or asymmetrical, unilateral or bilateral.

Most patients present with an asymptomatic nodular goiter but the goiter can be diffuse without palpable nodules. The goiter may be very large and extend to substernal area. Some patients experience a feeling of pressure in the neck; sudden pain and pressure suggest hemorrhage into a nodule.

There is typically no significant lymphadenopathy. Pressure on adjacent structures can lead to dysphagia due to esophageal compression. Pressure may also lead to a change in voice and choking secondary to vocal cord palsy. These are rare symptoms and suggest malignancy.

Raising arms above the head for a few minutes may induce congestion and redness of the face, dyspnea, and stridor indicating significant compression of the superior vena cava and other structures in the upper mediastinum (Pemberton's sign).
Patients are typically euthyroid, but subclinical or overt hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism can occur.
Goiter size tends to be underestimated when large and overestimated when small.

Neck ultrasonography is the first step in evaluating goiter and it differentiates diffuse from nodular goiter. It is extremely helpful to assess nodules in terms of size and presence of any suspicious feature of malignancy, such as abnormal calcifications or increased vascularity.

Order serum TSH to assess thyroid hormone status. If the result is abnormal, a free thyroxine level (FT4) is indicated (and T3 is indicated if the FT4 level is normal). Most patients are euthyroid. A low TSH makes malignancy less likely but does not exclude it.
Fine-needle aspiration biopsy is recommended for suspicious thyroid nodules (eg, very firm, large, adherent, or suspicious on ultrasonography).

For most patients, TSH and fine-needle aspiration biopsy (if indicated as mentioned above) are the only tests needed. However, some patients need one or more of the following tests: Thyroid autoantibodies (antithyroid peroxidase and antithyroglobulin antibodies) are indicated if autoimmune thyroid disease is suspected, but they are typically negative in multinodular goiter. Anterior, posterior, and lateral view chest X-rays can confirm tracheal deviation and compression. CT scan or MRI of the neck can help whether surgery is contemplated to identify the extent of goiter and its relationship to adjacent structures. Flow volume loops can help to identify extrathoracic or intrathoracic tracheal compression leading to compromise of airflow.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation.
Most patients can be observed without intervention. C
Thyroid hormone suppression is generally not indicated as it is of limited effectiveness, especially in iodine-sufficient areas. B
Radioiodine ablation with or without recombinant TSH stimulation is an effective option for large goiters, especially in the elderly and those who are not surgical candidates. B

Surgery is considered for goiters causing pressure symptoms, in cases when malignancy cannot be excluded with fine-needle aspiration, and for cosmetic reasons. Total thyroidectomy may be more effective than subtotal thyroidectomy in reducing recurrence of goiter.B
Adequate iodine supplementation and the removal of any potential goitrogens (eg, drugs) are important general measures, especially in managing endemic goiter.

In asymptomatic nontoxic multinodular goiter, apart from adequate iodine intake and the removal of potential goitrogens, there is no indication for medical or surgical intervention, and expectant follow-up is adequate.

In the case of goiter with normal thyroid function, thyroid hormone suppressive therapy has a variable but generally limited effect on the size of the goiter; it can precipitate hyperthyroidism and is generally not indicated.

If thyroid hormone suppressive therapy is used, close follow-up is important to monitor response and to avoid overt hyperthyroidism. If no response to thyroid hormone suppressive therapy is seen after approximately 6 months, this therapy should be discontinued.

For patients with subclinical or overt hypothyroidism or in case thyroid suppressive treatment is initiated, use levothyroxine 25 to 50 μg/day, increasing by 25 to 50 μg/day at 6-week intervals until the TSH is normal. The usual dose is approximately 1 to 1.6 μg/kg/day.
Indications for surgery are rare and include significant pressure symptoms, suspicion of malignancy that cannot be ruled out by fine-needle aspiration biopsy, and cosmetic reasons.

Subtotal or total thyroidectomy are the surgeries of choice as there is a high risk of recurrence with less extensive surgery. Based on moderate certainty evidence, a Cochrane review concluded that total thyroidectomy may be more effective than subtotal thyroidectomy in reducing recurrence of goiter, but data on other important outcomes (e.g., reinterventions due to recurrence, adverse events, thyroid cancer incidence) is limited.
A systematic review of 14 studies concluded that pre-operative fine-needle aspiration is 88% accurate compared with final histology and should be considered prior to surgery.

There is insufficient evidence for the role of intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) compared to visual nerve identification in preventing recurrent laryngeal nerve injury among adults undergoing thyroid surgery.
A meta-analysis found that a cervical approach alone was used in 88% of patients with substernal gointer. These patients had a high rate of tracheal compression (61%).

In asymptomatic nontoxic multinodular goiter, apart from adequate iodine intake and the removal of potential goitrogens, there is no indication for medical or surgical intervention, and expectant follow-up is adequate.
Radioactive iodine ablation is an alternative option and can obviate the need for surgery, especially in elderly or high-risk patients.

Stimulation with recombinant TSH to increase radioiodine uptake by the goiter may result in more effective regression of the size of the goiter and minimize the radioiodine dose. A Cchrane review of six RCTs found it effective for reducing thyroid volume but resulted to higher rates of hypothyroidism compared to radioiodine alone. Data on quality of life and costs were insufficient.
Significant expansion of the size of the goiter after radioiodine therapy leading to more pressure can occur, especially when recombinant TSH is used.

A small percentage of patients may develop features of autoimmune thyroid disease after ablation (a clinical picture similar to that of Graves' disease with hyperthyroidism and positive thyroid antibodies).
Refer the patient if he or she has significant pressure symptoms or when there is a possibility of malignancy.
Also consider referral if there is a significant increase in size during follow-up, or if surgical or radioiodine therapy is indicated.
Most patients remain stable and can be followed up without intervention. B
Approximately 20% to 50% of thyroid nodules show some growth during long-term follow-up. B
Approximately 10% to 20% of patients with thyroid nodules may become subclinically or overtly hyperthyroid during long-term follow-up. B
Clinical assessment and measurements of serum TSH in 6-month to 12-month intervals is a reasonable follow-up strategy for the majority of patients. C
Nontoxic multinodular goiter usually remains stable in size, although nodules can grow slowly over time.
A large percentage of nontoxic multinodular goiters eventually and gradually acquire some autonomy over time, leading to subclinical or overt hyperthyroidism.

Multinodular goiters do not generally change to malignant tumors, but the risk of malignancy in a multinodular goiter at the initial evaluation is similar to the risk in single adenomas (approximately 4%-5%).
Approximately 20% to 50% of thyroid nodules may show some growth during long-term follow-up.
Approximately 10% to 20% of patients with thyroid nodules may become subclinically or overtly hyperthyroid during long-term follow-up.

Goiters can also disappear over time; in the Whickham study, a goiter was present in 15.5% of the population and at the 20-year follow-up, 20% of women and 5% of men in that cohort no longer had a goiter. However, 4% of the women and none of the men who initially had no goiters developed goiters during follow-up.
For the vast majority of patients with a nontoxic multinodular goiter, there are no significant ill effects from their goiters and they live normally.
Subclinical or overt hyperthyroidism or significant growth may occur and periodic assessment is essential.
In general, for patients who are asymptomatic, clinical evaluation every 6 to 12 months is adequate.
Measure serum TSH once to twice per year because some nodules may become functional and cause toxic multinodular goiter.
